summary: Try cap moo (แคบหมู), northern Thai fried pork skin, at a ground-floor food stall in Warorot Market (Kad Luang). It is especially good with nam prik noom (roasted green-chilli dip) and sticky rice; stalls sell different styles, including lean puffs and pieces with fat attached.
whyGo: Taste a classic Chiang Mai snack in the market where northern foods are sold by weight and bagged to take away.
Pair the airy crunch with smoky, sometimes hot nam prik noom for a more distinctive local tasting than eating the crackling alone.
bestFor: Pork eaters who enjoy crunchy, salty snacks and want a small, flexible market tasting.
Visitors who want an easy edible souvenir; sealed bags travel more easily than fresh market dishes.
skipIf: You avoid pork, need vegetarian or halal food, or have a pork-related allergy or dietary restriction.
You need a reliably low-fat snack: some cap moo retains a layer of fat, and stall ingredients and preparation vary.
duration: Allow 20–45 minutes to browse and buy a snack, or around an hour if you sit upstairs or combine it with another market tasting; estimates only.
cost: No current cap-moo price list was found. A Chiang Mai shopper reported buying the smallest bag for ฿20 at Thanin Market in 2021; treat that as an old comparison, not a Kad Luang quote. Ask the stall for the bag size and price before buying, and carry small baht notes.
hours: The Tourism Authority of Thailand Japan lists Warorot Market at 90 Wichayanon Road: Mon/Wed/Sun 05:00–18:00, Tue 10:30–18:00 and Thu–Sat 09:00–18:00. Stall hours and holiday changes vary; food choice is best earlier, not at closing.
bestTime: Visit in the morning or around lunchtime, before the main market winds down. The exact time freshly fried cap moo is available depends on the vendor; ask which batch is freshest.
gettingThere: Use “Kad Luang” or “Warorot Market” with a red songthaew or ride-hail. TAT lists about 10–20 minutes from central Chiang Mai and about 20 minutes from the railway station by car or songthaew. From Tha Phae Gate it is roughly a 1.3 km walk; allow extra time for traffic and crossings.
booking: No booking or admission is indicated. Buy by bag or weight at a ground-floor food stall; ask the price before the vendor packs it. For a seated accompaniment, the market has an upstairs food court, though the crackling stalls mainly sell takeaway goods.
accessibility: The main food stalls are on the ground floor. A recent visitor guide describes crowded, narrow aisles; it reports an escalator from the ground floor to the first upper floor, but no confirmed lift, and stairs elsewhere. Step-free access to all areas is unverified; ask locally for the easiest entrance and expect busy walkways.
practicalTips: Try cap moo with nam prik noom and sticky rice; ask whether pieces are lean (ไร้มัน) or have fat attached (ติดมัน) if texture or richness matters.
Ask for a sample if offered, and choose a dry, crisp bag with a good seal if taking it away. Freshness and storage practices vary by stall.
This is pork skin, often fried in pork fat; it is not suitable for vegetarians, vegans or people avoiding pork. Ask about shared utensils and other ingredients for allergy concerns.
Market vendors may not have English ingredient or allergen information. Pointing, showing the Thai name แคบหมู, and confirming the price are practical ways to order.
decemberNotes: December is a popular Chiang Mai travel period, so the market may feel busy, especially around weekends and year-end. No December 2026 vendor schedule or holiday hours have been published in the sources reviewed. Go earlier in the day and recheck the market listing shortly before visiting.
uncertainties: Current stall-specific prices, portion sizes and daily frying times were not published; the ฿20 example is from a 2021 personal report about Thanin Market, not Kad Luang.
The TAT market schedule may change, and each vendor may use different hours; December 2026 holiday operations are not confirmed.
Market accessibility, food handling standards and allergen controls are not formally documented in the sources reviewed.
